deck.title: NodeVideo Expression Loop — trust through typed execution

brief.prompt: Create exactly 5 slides. Explain NodeVideo's architecture and its most important design tradeoff.
brief.purpose: The interviewer can restate the system boundary, request flow, reliability mechanism, tradeoff, and honest proof boundary.
successCriteria: Preserve the approved five-part explanation exactly
Keep planning and execution boundaries visually explicit
Include failed proof and honest non-success states

slides.title: The problem is trust, not FFmpeg syntax
slides.notes:
This is an AI-narrated prototype of my backend interview answer. I built NodeVideo because generating FFmpeg was never the hard problem. Trust was. A model can understand intent and propose an edit, but frame math, encoding, and approval state must remain reviewable and reproducible.

Evidence pointers: docs/architecture.md:5-18; docs/architecture.md:64-71
Approved claim: A language model is useful for understanding creator intent and proposing an edit, but exact media execution needs a reviewable and reproducible boundary.

slides.title: Three planes, one typed handoff
slides.notes:
The architecture has three planes. NodeAgent owns intent, tool selection, retry policy, and explanation. Convex owns durable jobs, leases, checkpoints, versions, and approvals. Deterministic tools compile a typed EditPlan into fixed media operations. The web app controls the work; media workers execute it.

Evidence pointers: docs/architecture.md:36-71; docs/architecture.md:149-161
Approved claim: NodeAgent owns intent and orchestration, Convex owns durable coordination, and fixed tools compile typed plans into media outputs.

slides.title: The model plans; deterministic tools execute
slides.notes:
A request moves from brief to model proposal, then through approval to a hash-bound plan. Only then does fixed code perform cuts, crops, captions, and encoding. The plan cannot carry shell commands or an arbitrary FFmpeg graph. Durable state records what was proposed, accepted, and executed, so runs can replay or recover.

Evidence pointers: docs/architecture.md:149-161; convex/caseflow.ts:462-561; convex/lib/durability.ts:78-203; src/lib/browser-edit-plan-compiler.ts:399-543; scripts/workers/edit-plan-renderer.mjs:5-80
Approved claim: Requests move from brief to proposal to approval, then a hash-bound plan drives deterministic rendering and receipts.

slides.title: The tradeoff: less freedom, more inspectability
slides.notes:
The tradeoff is deliberate: less model freedom for more inspectability. New creative operations require versioned types and deterministic implementations. In return, stale proposals are rejected, concurrent workers are fenced by leases, digest mismatches fail closed, and interrupted review resumes from a checkpoint instead of silently mutating the timeline.

Evidence pointers: convex/caseflow.ts:246-396; convex/caseflow.ts:462-561; tests/unit/browser-ffmpeg.test.ts:118-180
Approved claim: NodeVideo trades unconstrained model flexibility for inspectability, reproducibility, bounded concurrency, and safer approval.

slides.title: Proof includes the failures
slides.notes:
The proof includes failure. Twenty-two targeted reliability tests pass. One integrated edit matched source identity on five of five phrases, but only one of five assigned cut boundaries met the timing gate, so the strict editorial verdict failed. That is the lesson: trustworthy agents need bounded state, explicit approval, deterministic execution, and honest non-success states. NodeVideo helps me say it; NodeSlide helps me show it.

Evidence pointers: targeted-test-receipt.json; docs/strict-editorial-audit.md:8-45
Approved claim: Current evidence proves bounded orchestration and deterministic mechanics, while honestly withholding generalized quality claims.
